title: Tokenized Kids: How We Charge Students to Think
author: Bauschard, Stefan
summary: Stefan Bauschard, a debate coach and educator, exposes a structural contradiction at the heart of American education: the activity that produces the most actual thinking -- competitive debate -- is among the few things schools charge families for, while the content-delivery machine (units, worksheets, test prep) is provided free. He argues that education's budget is its value statement, and the budget reveals that critical thinking and judgment, despite being the rhetorical north stars of every mission statement, are funded like hobbies rather than core curriculum. The article draws a sharp analogy between the economic structure of AI inference and the economic structure of access to deep thinking in schools: both are priced at near-zero for surface-level engagement and become expensive as reasoning deepens, with the bill falling on whoever can afford to pay for more tokens of thought. Bauschard argues this has created a two-tier cognition economy that predates AI and has been running inside public education for decades. He sharpens the contradiction by noting that AI Socratic tutors will be funded at scale by districts while the actual human Socratic tutor -- the debate coach doing the same work more effectively -- remains on a stipend or volunteers. His prescription is direct: if critical thinking is genuinely the mission, debate is curriculum, not extracurricular -- it must be staffed, funded, and free.
points: * The budget is the real value statement: schools fund content delivery universally (worksheets, test prep, the whole retrieval curriculum) but charge families for the one activity -- competitive debate -- that actually requires and builds reasoning, judgment, and critical thinking. * The AI inference analogy is structurally devastating: reasoning models charge more tokens for deeper thinking, and schools charge more dollars for deeper thinking -- both systems create a cognition premium that only the already-advantaged can sustain. * The contradiction is most visible in who is paid: AI Socratic tutors will be licensed at scale with institutional funding, while human Socratic tutors (debate coaches who do exactly what the software promises, more effectively) are paid stipends or work for free. * American schools have been running a two-tier cognition economy for decades -- every kid gets the worksheet (free tier: capped cognition), while depth of reasoning is reserved for those whose parents can fund the camp, the circuit, the private coach. * Bauschard's prescription: if critical thinking and human mentorship are genuinely sacred values, debate is curriculum -- not an extracurricular billed to parents; it must be staffed and funded the way AI learning summits are.
quotes: The single activity that produces the most actual thinking of anything we offer a teenager is the one thing we often make them pay for out of pocket.

You fund your priorities. You don't fundraise for them. The budget is the value statement, and right now the budget often says: content is the mission, and thinking is a hobby you can pursue if your parents can swing it.

We're getting ready to write enormous checks to AI companies for Socratic tutors -- software that will, supposedly, debate our kids, challenge their reasoning, ask the hard questions, build critical thinking at scale. Districts will find that money. Meanwhile, the human Socratic tutor is already in the building. She runs the debate team. She does the exact thing the software is promising -- for a stipend, after hours, while writing recommendation letters at 11pm.
The kid with the budget gets the camps, the coach, the circuit, the subscriptions -- the extended reasoning. The kid without it gets the worksheet and the free tier.

The nightmare everyone describes -- a cognitive elite that can afford the most powerful reasoning while everyone else gets throttled on the free tier -- isn't some future the machines are dragging us toward. It's a market we already built, by hand, and pointed at children.

We took the single most valuable thing we offer and made it the most exclusive. We put a paywall on critical thinking and judgment. The retrieval education stays universal -- every kid gets the worksheet -- while the thinking education quietly goes to the kids who could already afford it.
Kids shouldn't be selling donuts in the morning so they can think in the afternoon. The content is on the house. The thinking is extra.
